newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb special police say will stop guarding Karadzic.
newsitem.headline: Serb special police say will stop guarding Karadzic.

text.p: The chief of Bosnian Serb special police units promised on Friday to stop providing security for indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic in an agreement with NATO, alliance officers said.

Major General Goran Saric, head of the counter-terrorist brigade which helps guard Karadzic, signed the pact in the presence of British Lieutenant General Roderick Cordy-Simpson at the headquarters of the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Sarajevo.

"He was signing his understanding of the instructions and his intention to comply with those instructions," NATO spokesman Major John Blakeley told reporters. The peace force did not say exactly how much time Serb authorities had to carry out the agreement.
The paper signed by Saric was part of an effort by SFOR to hold senior police officers accountable for the actions of their men, Blakeley said.

It also followed hints of possible action by Western overseers of Bosnia's peace accords to seize indictees like Karadzic for handover to the U.N. war crimes tribunal after more than a year of caution and hesitation caused by fear of taking casualties.
NATO announced last week it was clamping down on the special police units which underpin Karadzic's authority in Bosnia's Serb territory.
The 2,000- to 3,000-strong special police brigade must now submit to rules set down by the alliance-led SFOR and related to post-war demilitarisation in Bosnia mandated by the 1995 peace treaty.

Under the new guidelines, the special police will no longer be allowed to employ weapons associated with military forces or to guard indicted war criminals such as Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb president.

The special police will be permitted to perform only those duties approved by SFOR, including protection for senior government officials, Blakeley said. "We will insist that the list of VIPs will first of all be approved by SFOR.
"Any person indicted for war crimes will not be protected by specialist police. That would be in contravention (of the guidelines) and appropriate measures would be taken," Blakeley said.

SFOR declined to discuss whether it had issued a deadline to Serb authorities to comply with the rules. "They will be given details and an appropriate amount of time to ensure that their forces are in compliance," he said.

SFOR has notified special police commanders across Serb territory of the rules and inspected stations housing the special police units, including a station in the eastern town of Janje which contains military-grade weaponry.

The move against the special police, dubbed "Operation Secure Beat", has angered nationalist Serb authorities close to Karadzic, who still wields power behind the scenes, but has so far produced no retaliatory violence against peacekeeping troops stationed in Serb territory.

A NATO swoop last month on two Serbs indicted for war crimes set off a wave of revenge bombings and attacks which Western officials blamed on nationalist hardliners loyal to Karadzic. The violence has since subsided.
